collab.question: When a Claude agent is picking a name for a new CSS class in this framework, what are the simple, foundational rules it should never break — and where are those rules genuinely just guidelines instead of hard rules?

fact.text: Never use a bare class name from framework.css's reserved list (flex, btn, card, page, etc.). The framework block is off-limits for anything new.
Always census the live CSS with grep before naming: grep -rhoE '\.<name>[a-z0-9-]*' public --include=*.css --include=*.js. A hit elsewhere is a collision and vetos the name.
Always prefix with the owning module (e.g., .panel-grip, not .grip) unless the selector already starts with the module's own class. This is the core collision-avoidance mechanism.
View class names ARE CSS class names—View.classify() kebab-cases every constructor in the chain. A bare class name like .stage needs the module prefix (.paging-stage, not just .stage).
A trailing dash in css-scopes.txt (e.g., ui-) reserves that namespace. Never create .ui-<thing> without owning ui- in the scopes file.
Page instance stamps use two dashes: .page--<slug>. Never start a new module class with page- (single dash) unless you ARE core/Page, to avoid collision with instance stamps.

When building a class name by concatenating data (e.g., '.module-' + variant.key), the module prefix goes INSIDE the string, and every possible value of the variable must pass the census, not just the literal in the source.
When opening a new namespace (a module's first class), add its prefix to css-scopes.txt. If you cannot write css-scopes.txt, record the reservation in the module's own doc/decisions.md under Open.

A core module that extends Page (not just core/Page itself) may take page-<module>- as a sub-namespace, declared in css-scopes.txt. This avoids collision with ext/layout's layout- and other realms' section-.

A bare word like .card (framework.css's padded surface) can coexist with many .card-* variants elsewhere, but framework.css is off-limits for new bare words—check it existed before naming anything -card or -tile.

If the CSS selector already starts with the module's class (e.g., .panel { ... .grip { } }), re-prefixing to .panel-grip is optional (the nesting provides the namespace). This is a guideline, not a rule.
The CSS census includes vendored bundles (e.g., minified three.js), so a grep hit does not always mean a collision. Look at WHERE the hit is and read the line; vendored code is no veto.
A bare line in css-scopes.txt (.flex, .card, .pad) reserves that exact class name AND any suffixed variant (.flex-*, .card-*, .pad-*); nothing else may use those names
A line ending with a dash (ui-, panel-, page-) reserves a namespace for that module; new classes there are .prefix-<thing>, not bare or with different prefixes
The framework block (lines 5–67 of css-scopes.txt) is off limits — no new classes may be added there; additions belong in their owning module's namespace
Every new class must be prefixed with its owning module's namespace (.panel-grip, not .grip) unless the selector already contains the module's own class

View subclasses automatically mint CSS class names via View.classify() — a class Stage becomes .stage, LayoutsPair becomes .layouts-pair; these minted names must be prefixed like any declared class (PagingStage → .paging-stage)

When building a class name by concatenating a variable (type-anchors-post + variant.key), the module prefix must be inside the string ('type-anchors-' + key), not just typed literally; test every possible variable value against the census

The page instance stamp uses TWO dashes (.page--<slug>), so never start a module class with single page- unless you are core/Page; core modules extending Page may take page-<module>- as a sub-namespace

When opening a new module namespace, add one line to css-scopes.txt (prefix-   /owner); if css-scopes.txt is outside your write fence, document it in the module's doc/decisions.md under Open so the next agent finds it
Before naming a -card, -tile, or -box class, check that .card is not already in use as a framework.css spacing word (a padded surface primitive, distinct from .pad and em-based controls)

Census the live CSS with grep to detect collisions: grep -rhoE "\.<name>[a-z0-9-]*" public --include=*.css --include=*.js | sort -u; a hit in another module vetoes the name, but check WHERE the hit is first (vendored bundles like three.js may match unrelated words)
List every View class you declare (grep -n 'class [A-Z]' your files) and check each minted name against the census; View.classify() turns constructor chains into kebab-case classes automatically

Three spacing words are framework primitives: .pad (page region), .card (framed box), and em-based sizing for controls and rows; these are not optional variants and predate hand-rolled -tile/-box classes

The rules do not specify precedence when multiple prefixes could apply, which retired classes (if any) should be scavenged, or whether certain compound modifiers on bare classes (.tabs.underline) follow different rules

Never introduce a bare class name that matches a reserved prefix line in css-scopes.txt (e.g. 'flex', 'card', 'page') without owning that module — the framework block is off limits entirely for anything new.
Always prefix a new class with its owning module's prefix (e.g. '.panel-grip', not '.grip') unless the selector already starts with the module's own class.

Before naming a class, grep-census the live CSS/JS for that name; a hit in another module is a collision and you must pick a different name — but check WHERE the hit is first, since vendored bundles (e.g. minified three.js) can false-positive.

A View subclass's constructor name is itself a CSS class (classify() kebab-cases the chain), so a class named Stage silently wears the framework's own '.stage' — check every view class name against the census too, not just literal class= strings.

A modifier class built by string concatenation (e.g. 'type-anchors-post ' + variant.key) is a class name too — put the module prefix inside the concatenated string itself, not just around it, and check every possible runtime value of the variable, not only the one literal visible in source.

Never start a new module's class with 'page-' unless the module is core/Page itself, since that is core/Page's reserved namespace — except a second core module that itself extends Page may register its own sub-namespace like 'page-layout-' or 'page-section-' in css-scopes.txt.

'page--<slug>' (two dashes) is the per-route instance stamp core/Page.class.js puts on every page, and it is a fixed, hard-coded convention — never repurpose the two-dash form for a different module's own naming.

When a module opens a new namespace, its first class must add one line to css-scopes.txt ('prefix-   owner'); if css-scopes.txt is outside your write fence, the reservation is still owed — write it into the module's own doc/decisions.md under Open instead of dropping it.

Before naming a '-card'/'-tile'/'-box' class, check it isn't just the framework's existing '.card' (a framed box) — the three spacing words are '.pad' for a page region, '.card' for a framed box, and an em unit for a control or row; ~180 hand-rolled duplicate card/tile classes existed sitewide before this was enforced.

It is only a guideline, not a hard rule, exactly which of '.pad' / '.card' / an em-based size a given box should use — the skill gives a rule of thumb (page region vs framed box vs control/row) but real layouts have judgment calls at the edges.
Skipping the whole new-css-class check is allowed, but only when reusing a class name that already exists — any genuinely new or renamed class name must go through the check.

One component gets one prefix used consistently for all its sub-parts (e.g. ui-<component>-*, panel-*, sidebar-*) rather than a fresh ad hoc name per sub-part — this is the general shape of every registered entry in css-scopes.txt, though the file does not state it as an explicit numbered rule.

haiku-c: # CSS Class Naming: Rules That Break vs. Guidelines for Judgment
sonnet-b: # Naming a new CSS class in this framework: rules vs guidelines (revised)

vote.caveat: Both answers are solid, but sonnet-b's deeper exploration of the 'optional' re-prefixing risk (warning that nesting doesn't provide collision safety, only selector organization) and its proposal to document 'more specific prefix wins' as a stated default convention are more useful than the alternatives. One small improvement: rank the five hard rules by criticality — the live census check is the one mechanism that catches hidden class names and should come first.

The guideline section is clearer on why 'optional' is misleading and proposes a longest-prefix convention for precedence; the one improvement would be shortening the repetition about 'optional' — the heading and the caveat say similar things, and both say it again in the bottom line.
It restates the census grep command inline, which risks going stale if the skill's command ever changes — better to point at the skill step number than re-embed the exact command.
